ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Rubella virus infection during early pregnancy can cause congenital rubella syndrome, presenting with sensorineural deafness, cataracts, heart defects and blueberry‑muffin rash. Early recognition and prevention are key.

sections.p: Rubella is a togavirus transmitted by respiratory droplets. In pregnancy, especially the first trimester, it can cross the placenta and damage the fetus.
b: Mild rash in children; severe in fetus

sections.p: Rubella is a single‑stranded, positive‑sense RNA virus with a lipid envelope. It replicates in the cytoplasm and spreads via respiratory secretions.
Human-to-human spread through droplets; incubation 14–21 days. The virus infects epithelial cells, spreads to lymphoid tissue, then to the fetus via the placenta.

Congenital rubella syndrome (CRS) results from maternal infection in the first trimester. Classic triad: sensorineural deafness, cataracts, patent ductus arteriosus. Other findings include blueberry‑muffin rash, hepatosplenomegaly, growth restriction.
Diagnosis is clinical plus laboratory confirmation. Maternal serology (IgM, IgG) and PCR; fetal ultrasound for structural anomalies; newborn hearing and eye exams.

t.b: Positive IgM indicates recent infection; supports CRS risk
IgG alone suggests past infection; absence of IgM reduces CRS risk

t.a: PCR of maternal or fetal sample
t.b: Detects viral RNA; confirms active infection
Reveals PDA or other congenital heart defects

sections.p: No specific antiviral for rubella. Management focuses on supportive care and prevention of complications. Vaccination of women of childbearing age is the cornerstone of control.

t.b: Prevents maternal infection; contraindicated in pregnancy

sections.p: Remember the classic triad and blueberry‑muffin rash. Maternal infection before 20 weeks carries the highest risk. Prevention via vaccination is the most effective strategy.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe hearing loss, cataracts, heart murmurs, or unexplained rash in a newborn

faq.q: Can rubella be treated with antivirals?
faq.a: No specific antiviral exists; treatment is supportive.

faq.q: Is the MMR vaccine safe in pregnancy?
faq.a: No, it is a live vaccine and is contraindicated during pregnancy.
It is extramedullary hematopoiesis seen as purplish skin lesions in infants with CRS.
